https://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/libra.text: Military WMD Menu Introduction Systems Facilities Agencies Operations Countries Hot Documents News Reports Policy Budget Congress Links Intelligence Homeland Security Space Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) Foreign Minister Tsahkna: Sanctions package initiated by Senator Graham would deliver a powerful blow to Russia's economy Republic of Estonia - Ministry of Foreign Affairs 18.07.2026 | 09:55 This week it was confirmed that the Russia sanctions bill introduced in the U.S. Senate by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal has secured the support of more than 60 senators as well as the White House. The package aims to impose tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas or assist Moscow in circumventing existing sanctions. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna welcomed the Senate initiative, stressing that approval of the sanctions package would deal a significant blow to Russia's economy. "Energy exports play a central role in financing Russia's war machine, accounting for nearly one third of the aggressor's state budget," Tsahkna said. "Late Senator Lindsey Graham proposed imposing tariffs on countries that contribute to Russia's aggression or facilitate the operations of its shadow fleet. This is an important step that directly undermines Russia's economic capacity and reduces the revenue Moscow can channel into continuing its aggression against Ukraine. We commend the U.S. senators for this groundbreaking proposal." According to Tsahkna, the international community — including the European Union and the United States — must continue exerting pressure on Moscow until Russia stops bombing Ukraine and killing civilians, abandons its imperial ambitions, and takes accountability for the crimes it has committed. He emphasized that EU member states must overcome the current deadlock and approve a robust 21st sanctions package, which would, among other measures, keep the price cap on Russian crude oil at a consistently low level. "Sanctions and international isolation are working: Russia's economy is clearly deteriorating, internal tensions are rising, and Ukraine is achieving significant strategic gains on the battlefield. Russia will not abandon its aggressive course until countermeasures inflict truly painful consequences. Pressure on the aggressor must therefore remain steady and unwavering. This is not the moment for concessions," Tsahkna stressed. In addition to measures targeting countries that import Russian energy, the sanctions package includes restrictions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, other senior officials, financial institutions, state-owned enterprises, and companies supporting Russia's defense industry. The next step is approval by the full Senate.

Overnight Ukraine was once again affected by Russian attacks, which killed at least three in the eastern city of Kharkiv. 370,000 people were left without power in the Volyn region bordering Poland. Today’s talks come at a critical moment as Ukraine increasingly struggles with repelling Russian air attacks as a result of acute shortages of interceptor missiles, with Zelenskyy also involved in a very public series of disagreements with Donald Trump at White House. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters Japan Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa Ramon Antonio Vargas and agencies Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.41 EDT First published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 08.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported . Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges. Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on Okinawa Read more NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings. Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported. While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported. A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”. “She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.” Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based. Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies. A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s. In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman. US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61. The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972. There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high. After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.” Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting Explore more on these topics Japan US military US crime Asia Pacific news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
